### TCW/E-SB24 · Banū Saʿd stayed out, and ʿAlī ؓ said so
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, days after the battle `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** البصرة.

**What happened:** After the battle the notables of Basra came in to ʿAlī ؓ. Among them was
al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays, at the head of Banū Saʿd, and they had kept out of the fighting altogether. ʿAlī ؓ
did not let it pass. He said one word to him: you held back. Al-Aḥnaf answered at length and
did not apologise. He said he thought he had done well, that what had happened had happened by the
caliph's own order, and that ʿAlī ؓ would need him tomorrow more than he had needed him yesterday.

**The statement:**
> فقال له علي: تربصت (٣) - (يعني) بنا- فقال: ما كنتُ أراني إلا قد (٤) أحسنت، وبأمرك كان ما كان يا أمير المؤمنين، فارفق فإن طريقك الذي سلكت بعيد، وأنت إليَّ غداً أحوج منك أمس، فاعرف إحساني، واستبق مودتي لغد
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۲۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3571
> *English:* "ʿAlī said to him: You held back — [that is,] from us. He said: I did not see myself as having done anything but well; and what happened was by your order, O Commander of the Faithful. So be gentle, for the road you have taken is long, and you will need me tomorrow more than you needed me yesterday. So acknowledge my good service, and keep my affection in reserve for tomorrow."

**عبرت:** He did not plead illness and he did not plead scruple. He argued that his restraint was a
service, and asked to be thanked for it.

### TCW/E-SB25 · Two books, two pictures of the same man
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36–37 AH `[SOURCED, the books differ]` · **Map:** البصرة, then صفين.

**What happened:** Al-Aḥnaf appears on most popular lists of the men who would not fight, and our
own two books will not both put him there. Ibn Kathīr twice describes his people as having withdrawn
from the fighting at the Camel — the second time, as having withdrawn from the two parties. Al-Dhahabī, opening the man's own biography, states without
qualification that he was one of the commanders of ʿAlī's army at Ṣiffīn. Nothing on either page
reconciles the two, and the honest telling gives both.

**The statement:**
> كَانَ مِنْ قُوَّادِ جَيْشِ عَلِيٍّ يَوْمَ صِفِّيْنَ.
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۴ ص۸۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/3240
> *English:* "He was one of the commanders of ʿAlī's army on the day of Ṣiffīn."

**عبرت:** A man can stand out of one fight and stand in the next, and a careful account says so
rather than tidying him into one or the other.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB26 · Silence in a room where truth is dangerous
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** not dated on the page; معاوية ؓ is spoken of as living `[STANDARD]`
*(to verify)* · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Men in a gathering were saying things about Muʿāwiya ؓ, and al-Aḥnaf sat through
it without a word. Someone finally asked him why he was not speaking. His answer is one line of
Arabic and it is the whole predicament of a public man in a bad season.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ: أَخْشَى اللهَ إِنْ كَذَبْتُ، وَأَخْشَاكُم إِنْ صَدَقْتُ.
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۴ ص۹۲ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/3245
> *English:* "He said: I fear God if I lie, and I fear you if I tell the truth."

**عبرت:** There are rooms in which silence is the only honest thing left, and a man should know when
he is in one.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB27 · Abū Mūsā ؓ did not fight alongside ʿAlī ؓ
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36–38 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** الكوفة, then أذرح.

**What happened:** Of all the men who would not fight, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī ؓ paid the highest price
in reputation, and al-Dhahabī says so directly while explaining where the hostility comes from. He
gives two reasons, and it is the first that belongs to this evening. The man did not fight alongside
ʿAlī ؓ. The second reason is what happened afterwards, when ʿAlī ؓ made him arbitrator over himself.

**The statement:**
> وَلاَ رَيْبَ أَنَّ غُلاَةَ الشِّيْعَةِ يُبْغِضُوْنَ أَبَا مُوْسَى -رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ- لِكَوْنِهِ مَا قَاتَلَ مَعَ عَلِيٍّ
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2374
> *English:* "There is no doubt that the extremists of the Shīʿa hate Abū Mūsā — may God be pleased with him — because he did not fight alongside ʿAlī."

**عبرت:** What standing out of the fighting cost these men came later, in the telling, and it was
their reputations that paid it.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB28 · The arbitrator names the man who would not fight
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 37–38 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** أذرح · المدينة.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabī puts the whole outcome of the arbitration into one clause, and it is
the tightest summary in either book. Abū Mūsā ؓ removed ʿAlī ؓ, and removed Muʿāwiya ؓ, and then
pointed to a third man as the way out. The man he pointed to was Ibn ʿUmar ؓ — the one who had held
his hand back and never regretted it. And al-Dhahabī closes the sentence with a clause about what
came of it.

**The statement:**
> ثُمَّ لَمَّا حَكَّمَهُ عَلِيٌّ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ عَزَلَهُ، وَعَزَلَ مُعَاوِيَةَ، وَأَشَارَ بِابْنِ عُمَرَ؛ فَمَا انْتَظَمَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ حَالٌ.
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2374
> *English:* "And then, when ʿAlī made him arbitrator over himself, he deposed him and deposed Muʿāwiya, and pointed to Ibn ʿUmar — and no state of affairs came right out of that."

**عبرت:** The way out that was offered was a man nobody had a quarrel with, and by then it was too
late for a man nobody had a quarrel with.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB29 · Judge, even to the cutting of my neck
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 37–38 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Before the arbitration, ʿAlī ؓ gave his arbitrator his instructions. They were
one line long. He did not tell him what to find, and he did not tell him what to protect. He told
him to judge, and he named the worst thing the judgement could cost, and told him to judge anyway.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ أَبُو صَالِحٍ السَّمَّانُ: قَالَ عَلِيٌّ: يَا أَبَا مُوْسَى، احْكُمْ، وَلو عَلَى حَزِّ
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2375
> عُنُقِي (١) .
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2376
> *English:* "Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān said: ʿAlī said: O Abū Mūsā, judge — even if it be to the cutting of my neck."

**عبرت:** He handed a man the authority to rule against him and told him to use it.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB30 · Two provinces for two sons, refused in writing
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 37–40 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** الكوفة · البصرة · دمشق.

**What happened:** Muʿāwiya ؓ wrote to Abū Mūsā ؓ with an offer, in his own hand, and asked for an
answer in Abū Mūsā ؓ's own hand so that it could not later be denied. ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ ؓ had already
agreed. If Abū Mūsā ؓ agreed too, one of his sons would have Kūfa and the other would have Basra,
and no door would ever be closed to him again. Abū Mūsā ؓ wrote back briefly. He did not
argue. He asked one question, and it was not about this world.

**The statement:**
> فَكَتَبَ إِلَيْهِ: أَمَّا بَعْدُ، فَإِنَّكَ كَتَبْتَ إِلَيَّ فِي جَسِيْمِ أَمْرِ الأُمَّةِ، فَمَاذَا أَقُوْلُ لِرَبِّي إِذَا قَدِمْتُ عَلَيْهِ، لَيْسَ لِي فِيْمَا عَرَضْتَ مِنْ حَاجَةٍ، وَالسَّلاَمُ عَلَيْكَ.
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2376
> *English:* "So he wrote back to him: To proceed — you have written to me concerning a weighty matter of this umma. What shall I say to my Lord when I come before Him? I have no need of what you have offered. And peace be upon you."

**عبرت:** The charge against every man who would not take a side is that he was waiting for the best
offer. Here is the best offer, in writing, and here is the answer.

**Hands-up?** Two governorships for his two sons, and an open door for life. What would you write
back?

### TCW/E-SB31 · What the historian concluded about him in the end
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** the closing of his ترجمة `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabī has recorded the hostility, the arbitration, the whole difficult
story. He places his own verdict immediately after the letter to Muʿāwiya ؓ, as the last word of the
whole life, and it is a list of qualities with one clause at the end about what office did to
him.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: قَدْ كَانَ أَبُو مُوْسَى صَوَّاماً، قَوَّاماً، رَبَّانِيّاً، زَاهِداً، عَابِداً، مِمَّنْ جَمَعَ العِلْمَ وَالعَمَلَ وَالجِهَادَ وَسَلاَمَةَ الصَّدْرِ، لَمْ تُغَيِّرْهُ الإِمَارَةُ، وَلاَ اغْتَرَّ بِالدُّنْيَا.
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2376
> *English:* "I say: Abū Mūsā was much-fasting, much-praying, a man of the Lord, ascetic, devoted in worship — one of those who gathered knowledge, action, jihād, and soundness of breast. Command did not change him, nor was he deluded by this world."

**عبرت:** The scholars of this ummah knew everything the critics knew, and this is still where they
finished.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB32 · The man who stood aside got the treasury
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** البصرة.

**What happened:** When ʿAlī ؓ organised the government of Basra after the battle he put Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ
over the city and set another man over the land tax and the treasury beside him, and told Ibn
ʿAbbās ؓ to listen to him. Ibn Kathīr adds one clause about that man as he names him, and the clause
is the point. He had been one of those who stood aside.

**The statement:**
> وجعل معه زياد بن أبيه على الخراج وبيت المال، وأمر ابن عباس أن يسمع من زياد -وكان زياد معتزلًا-
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۲۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3572
> *English:* "And he set Ziyād ibn Abīhi with him over the land tax and the treasury, and ordered Ibn ʿAbbās to listen to Ziyād — and Ziyād had been one who stood aside."

**عبرت:** Nobody was punished for having stayed out. Two of them were offered the province and a
third was given the money.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB33 · Ten thousand at Khirbitā, and a truce instead
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** مصر · خِرْبتا near الإسكندرية.

**What happened:** Egypt gave the pledge to ʿAlī ؓ except for one place. At a village called
Khirbitā, near Alexandria, about ten thousand men would not — and the account is careful to say who
they were, the leaders of the people and their notables, not a rabble. They sent to ʿAlī ؓ's own
governor, and the governor made a truce with them rather than fight them. One other man of the
Anṣār stayed out of the pledge separately, and he too was left alone.

**The statement:**
> واستقامت له طاعة بلاد مصر سوى قرية منها يقال لها خِرْبتا (٤)، فيها ناس قد أعظموا قتل عثمان - وكانوا سادة الناس ووجوههم وكانوا في نحو من عشرة آلاف … وبعثوا إلى قيس بن سعد فوادعهم
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3581
> *English:* "The obedience of the land of Egypt was settled for him, except for one village of it called Khirbitā, in which were people who held the killing of ʿUthmān to be a grave thing — and they were the leaders of the people and their notables, and they were about ten thousand … They sent to Qays ibn Saʿd, and he made a truce with them."

**عبرت:** Refusing to take a side was not the private scruple of four famous men. In one province it
was ten thousand of the leading men at once.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB34 · A governor asks to be replaced rather than attack
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36–37 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** مصر.

**What happened:** Later the order came from ʿAlī ؓ to Qays ibn Saʿd ؓ to go and fight the men of
Khirbitā who had stayed out of the pledge. Qays ؓ wrote back with his reasons — that they were many
and that they were the notables of the people — and then made the offer that ends the argument. If
the order had been given to test his loyalty, then let someone else be sent to Egypt in his place.
He was replaced. He went to Medina, then to ʿAlī ؓ, and made his excuse, and it was accepted, and he
fought at Ṣiffīn.

**The statement:**
> وكتب إليه: إن كنت إنما أمرتني بهذا لتختبرني لأنك اتَّهمتني [في طاعتك]، فابعث على عملك بمصر غيري
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۳۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3582
> *English:* "And he wrote to him: If you have ordered me to do this only to test me, because you suspected me [in your obedience], then send someone other than me over your work in Egypt."

**عبرت:** He would rather lose the province than open a second war inside it, and the caliph took
his resignation and kept his friendship.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB35 · Men who hid rather than march
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** not dated on the page; 36 AH `[STANDARD]` *(to verify)* ·
**Map:** الكوفة.

**What happened:** When ʿAlī ؓ marched out of Kūfa he left Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī ؓ in charge of the
city. The moment the army was gone, men who had not gone with it came out of hiding — or rather went
into it, because the report says they hid themselves. Abū Masʿūd ؓ went up on the pulpit and called
them out by the fact of their hiding, and told them to show themselves.

**The statement:**
> لَمَّا خَرَجَ عَلِيٌّ، اسْتَخْلَفَ أَبَا مَسْعُوْدٍ عَلَى الكُوْفَةِ، وَتَخَبَّأَ رِجَالٌ لَمْ يَخْرُجُوا مَعَ عَلِيٍّ.
> فَقَالَ أَبُو مَسْعُوْدٍ عَلَى المِنْبَرِ: أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ، مَنْ كَانَ تَخَبَّأَ، فَلْيَظْهَرْ؛
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۴۹۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2476
> *English:* "When ʿAlī went out he left Abū Masʿūd in charge of Kūfa, and men hid themselves and did not go out with ʿAlī. Abū Masʿūd said from the pulpit: O people, whoever has hidden himself, let him show himself."

**عبرت:** There is a difference between a man who says openly that he will not fight and a man who
hides until the army has left, and the pulpit knew it.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB36 · One authority said four, the historian named six
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Shaʿbī, an early and respected authority, said that only four of the Prophet's ﷺ
Companions were at the Camel at all, and staked his own credit on it — produce a fifth, he said, and
I am a liar. Ibn Kathīr copies the statement into his book and then, in the next sentence and in his
own voice, produces six. He then offers a way of saving al-Shaʿbī's meaning, and marks it plainly as
a guess.

**The statement:**
> قال الشعبي: لم يشهد الجمل من أصحاب النبي ﷺ غير علي وعمّار وطلحة والزبير؛ فإن جاؤوا بخامس فأنا كذاب. قلت: قد حضرتها عائشة وابن الزبير والحسن والحسين ومحمد بن أبي بكر وسهل بن حنيف وآخرون.
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۲۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3573
> *English:* "Al-Shaʿbī said: none of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ was present at al-Jamal except ʿAlī, ʿAmmār, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr; and if they produce a fifth, then I am a liar. I say: ʿĀʾisha was present at it, and Ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, and Muḥammad ibn Abī Bakr, and Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, and others."

**عبرت:** This is what a history written with a conscience looks like: the source is copied in full
and corrected on the same page, in the open.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB37 · A famous report, examined and thrown away
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** after صفين; the page carries no year `[STANDARD]` *(to verify)* ·
**Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Ibn Kathīr reaches a report that is widely circulated about these years, one that
would settle a great deal if it were sound. He does not suppress it and he does not soften it. He
prints the whole thing, with its chain, exactly as he received it. Then, without a paragraph break,
he states what he thinks of it, names the single man in the chain who is the reason, and says what
the scholars of ḥadīth say about that man.

**The statement:**
> هذا السياق الظاهر أنه موضوع وآفته من جهة المعلى بن عبد الرحمن فإنه متروك الحديث، والله أعلم (٧).
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۵۱۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3662
> *English:* "This account is apparently a forgery, and its defect comes from the side of al-Muʿallā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, for he is abandoned in ḥadīth — and God knows best."

**عبرت:** The reports about this period were sifted a thousand years ago by men who had every reason
to want them true, and they threw away the ones that would not hold.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB38 · We narrated their anger and they made it religion
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** the second century AH `[STANDARD]` *(to verify — الأعمش's dates are
not on this page)* · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabī comes to a report in which one Companion appears to say something hard
about another. He prints it, because that is what an honest book does. Then he says, in his own
voice, that he does not know what the sense of the statement is. And then he quotes al-Aʿmash, who
had spent his life transmitting exactly this kind of material, saying what had happened to it in the
hands of the people who received it.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: مَا أَدْرِي مَا وَجْهُ هَذَا القَوْلِ … ثُمَّ يَقُوْلُ الأَعْمَشُ: حَدَّثْنَاهُمْ بِغَضَبِ أَصْحَابِ مُحَمَّدٍ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- فَاتَّخَذُوْهُ دِيْناً (٢) .
> — سیر أعلام النبلاء جـ۲ ص۳۹۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2374
> *English:* "I say: I do not know what the sense of this statement is … and then al-Aʿmash says: we narrated to them the anger of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and they took it as a religion."

**عبرت:** Words spoken in one bad hour between men who loved each other were collected by later
people and turned into a creed, and that is the whole disease of this chapter.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB39 · Let none of us reproach another
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** Saturday, the first of Rajab 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** البصرة → مكة,
arrow drawn.

**What happened:** On the first Saturday of Rajab, Umm al-Muʾminīn ؓ left Basra. ʿAlī ؓ had sent her
every provision she needed and forty women of the city to travel with her, and her own brother went
with her. He came and stood at the door while the people gathered, and she spoke to them from the
litter. She told them not to reproach one another, said what had been between herself and ʿAlī ؓ was
no more than what is between a woman and her husband's family, and said that he was among the best.
ʿAlī ؓ answered her in front of everybody. Then he walked beside her for some miles on the road, and
sent his sons on with her for the rest of the day.

**The statement:**
> وقالت: يا بنيَّ لا يعتب بعضنا على بعض (٥) … فقال علي: صدقتِ والله ما كان بيني وبينها إلا ذاك، وإنها لزوجةُ نبيكم ﷺ في الدنيا والآخرة.
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۲۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3572
> *English:* "And she said: My sons, let none of us reproach another … ʿAlī said: She has spoken the truth. By God, there was nothing between me and her but that — and she is the wife of your Prophet ﷺ in this world and the next."

**عبرت:** The two people with the most to say against each other closed it themselves, in public, and
left nothing for anybody else to carry on with.

**Hands-up?** no

### TCW/E-SB40 · A hundred lashes at the door
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** البصرة.

**What happened:** While ʿAlī ؓ was in the house where Umm al-Muʾminīn ؓ was staying, a man came to
tell him that there were two men at the door speaking against her. There was no debate about it. He
ordered al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn ʿAmr to give each of them a hundred lashes and to strip them of their clothes.
On the same visit a widow of the battle stood in front of him and cursed him to his face, twice, and
he answered her with silence, and told the man who objected that they had been ordered to hold back
from women when women were idolaters.

**The statement:**
> فقال له رجل: يا أمير المؤمنين إن على الباب رجلين ينالان من عائشة، فأمر عليٌّ القعقاعَ بن عمرو أن يجلدَ كلَّ واحدٍ منهما مئة وأن يخرجَهما من ثيابهما.
> — البدایہ والنہایہ جـ۷ ص۴۲۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/30097/3572
> *English:* "A man said to him: O Commander of the Faithful, there are two men at the door speaking against ʿĀʾisha. So ʿAlī ordered al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn ʿAmr to give each of them a hundred lashes and to strip them of their clothes."

**عبرت:** The line was drawn by the man who had just won the battle, and it was drawn against his own
supporters.

**Hands-up?** no

## The people: profiles I — عثمان ؓ's circle and the men of الجمل

*Source note: [`people-of-the-fitna-profiles-i.md`](../docs/research/people-of-the-fitna-profiles-i.md) — read it for the pages behind these cards.*

### POT/E-PF1 · The man of Taym who stood beside Abu Bakr's clan
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** before 23 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The first man the evening needs is a Companion of the same clan as Abu Bakr. Talha ibn Ubaydullah was of Banu Taym ibn Murra of Quraysh, the small clan that had already given the ummah its first caliph. He was one of the ten given the good news of Paradise, and one of the six men Umar left behind to choose his successor. His wife was Umm Kulthum, a daughter of Abu Bakr, which made him the brother-in-law of the Mother of the Believers Aisha. When the room later sees him riding towards Basra in her company, that clan tie is the whole explanation, and it needs nothing added to it.

**The statement:**
> none in the sources we use

**عبرت:** A man's place in a quarrel is often decided by his family long before it is decided by his opinion.

**Hands-up?** Who was the closest kinsman among the Companions to أبو بكر ؓ — by clan, not by blood?

---

### POT/E-PF2 · Three names given on three different days
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** before 23 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The tradition did not have to invent a title for this man. A report in the Siyar has the Prophet ﷺ giving him a different name on each of three days: at Uhud, Talha the Good; on the expedition of Dhu al-Ushayra, Talha the Open-handed; on the day of Khaybar, Talha the Generous. Al-Dhahabi records the report and then, in one word, tells the reader what its chain is worth: it is weak-ish. That is the honest way to use it, and it is how the speaker should use it too.

**The statement:**
> لَمَّا كَانَ يَوْمُ أُحُدٍ سَمَّاهُ النَّبِيُّ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-: طَلْحَةَ الخَيْرَ، وَفِي غَزْوَةِ ذِي العَشِيْرَةِ (٣) : طَلْحَةَ الفَيَّاضَ، وَيَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ: طَلْحَةَ الجُوْدَ (٤) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۰ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1456
> *English:* "On the day of أحد the Prophet ﷺ named him طلحة الخير; and at the expedition of ذو العشيرة, طلحة الفياض; and on the day of خيبر, طلحة الجود."

**عبرت:** A title the ummah remembers is worth more than one we would have invented, even when the chain that carries it is thin.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF3 · Umar asks Talha why he is unkempt and grieving
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** after 11 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** After the Prophet ﷺ died, Umar saw Talha unkempt and dust-coloured and put to him the blunt question: is it that the rule has gone to your cousin, meaning Abu Bakr? Talha's answer was God forbid, and he explained what was really eating him. He had heard the Prophet ﷺ say that he knew a word which no dying man says without his soul finding ease by it, and he had never asked him what the word was. Umar told him he knew it: it was the word the Prophet ﷺ offered his uncle. Talha said: you have spoken truly.

**The statement:**
> أَرَاكَ شَعِثْتَ وَاغْبرَرْتَ مُذْ تُوُفِّيَ رَسُوْلُ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-؟ لَعَلَّهُ أَنَّ مَا بِكَ إِمَارَةُ ابْنِ عَمِّكَ -يَعْنِي: أَبَا بَكْرٍ-.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۸ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1464
> *English:* "I see you have grown unkempt and dust-coloured since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died. Perhaps what is in you is the rule of your cousin — meaning أبو بكر."

**عبرت:** The suspicion a leader owes it to his brother to speak aloud is better out in the open than left to grow.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF4 · Twenty-four wounds and a man carried backwards
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 3 AH, Uhud `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina lights; Uhud beside it.

**What happened:** The room should meet Talha wounded before it meets him rich. At Uhud his sons counted twenty-four wounds on their father in one day: a square gash in his head, his sciatic vein cut, a finger crippled, and the rest of the wounds all over his body until he fainted. The Prophet, upon him be peace, had a tooth broken and his face gashed and was fainting himself. Talha carried him, walking backwards out of the press, and whenever a man of the enemy caught up he turned and fought him off, until he had him propped up in the ravine.

**The statement:**
> جُرِحَ أَبُوْنَا يَوْمَ أُحُدٍ أَرْبَعاً وَعِشْرِيْنَ جِرَاحَةً، وَقَعَ مِنْهَا فِي رَأْسِهِ شَجَّةٌ مُرَبَّعَةٌ، وَقُطِعَ نِسَاهُ -يَعْنِي العِرْقَ- وَشُلَّتْ أُصْبُعُهُ، وَكَانَ سَائِرُ الجِرَاحِ فِي جَسَدِهِ، وَغَلَبَهُ الغَشْيُ، وَرَسُوْلُ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- مَكْسُوْرَة رَبَاعِيَتُهُ، مَشْجُوْجٌ فِي وَجْهِهِ، قَدْ عَلاَهُ الغَشْيُ، وَطَلْحَةُ مُحْتَمِلُهُ يَرْجعُ بِهِ القَهْقَرَى، كُلَّمَا أَدْرَكَهُ أَحَدٌ مِنَ المُشْرِكِيْنَ، قَاتَلَ دُوْنَهُ، حَتَّى أَسْنَدَهُ إِلَى الشِّعْبِ (١) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۲ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1458
> *English:* "Our father was wounded at أحد with twenty-four wounds. Among them was a square gash in his head; his sciatic vein was cut, his finger was crippled, and the rest of the wounds were in his body, and faintness overcame him — while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had his tooth broken and his face gashed and faintness had come over him, and طلحة was carrying him, going backwards; whenever any of the polytheists caught up with him, he fought him off, until he propped him against the ravine."

**عبرت:** What a man does on the worst day of his life is the fact about him that should be told first.

**Hands-up?** How many wounds do you suppose one man can take in a single afternoon and live?

### POT/E-PF5 · The withered hand a man could still see years later
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** after 3 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The hand Talha put over the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud never worked again. Al-Bukhari carries the eyewitness line: Qays said he saw that hand with his own eyes, withered. It is short, it is authentic, and it is the kind of physical detail a room remembers for a year. It also fixes Talha in the mind before the difficult part of his story begins.

**The statement:**
> رَأَيْتُ يَدَ طَلْحَةَ الَّتِي وَقَى بِهَا النَّبِيَّ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- يَوْمَ أُحُدٍ شَلاَّءَ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۲۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1452
> *English:* "I saw the hand of طلحة, with which he shielded the Prophet ﷺ on the day of أحد, withered."

**عبرت:** Some services are paid for once and then carried in the body for the rest of a life.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF6 · The man who missed Badr and was given its reward
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 2 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Badr lights, then fades.

**What happened:** Talha was not at Badr. He was away in Syria on trade when the battle was fought, and he grieved over having missed the day that every early Muslim measured himself by. The Prophet, upon him be peace, assigned him his share of the spoils and his reward along with it. The detail matters because it settles, early and without argument, that a man's standing in this story is not the same thing as his attendance record.

**The statement:**
> none in the sources we use

**عبرت:** A man is credited with the good he intended and was kept from, not only with the good he was present for.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF7 · Seven hundred thousand, and a night without sleep
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** in Uthman's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Hadramawt lights on the map, then Medina.

**What happened:** Money came to Talha from Hadramawt: seven hundred thousand. He took it into his house and then could not sleep, turning over in bed all night. His wife asked him what was wrong. He told her he had been thinking since nightfall, and the thought was a question about himself: what is a man's opinion of his Lord, if he passes the night with this money sitting in his house? This is the richest Companion in the story, and the first thing the room learns about his wealth is that it kept him awake.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ: تَفَكَّرْتُ مُنْذُ اللَّيْلَةِ، فَقُلْتُ: مَا ظَنُّ رَجُلٍ بِرَبِّهِ يَبِيْتُ وَهَذَا المَالُ فِي بَيْتِهِ؟
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۱ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1457
> *English:* "He said: I have been thinking since last night, and I said — what is a man's opinion of his Lord, that he should pass the night with this money in his house?"

**عبرت:** Wealth is a trust that presses on the man who holds it, not a comfort he is owed.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF8 · The wife who told him to send for the bowls
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in Uthman's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** His wife's answer to the sleepless night was practical. Where are you, she said, from some of your friends? When morning comes, call for bowls and dishes and divide it. He said: God have mercy on you, you are rightly-guided, the daughter of a rightly-guided man. And the Siyar tells the reader who she was in the same breath: Umm Kulthum, the daughter of al-Siddiq. In the morning he called for the bowls and divided the whole sum among the Emigrants and the Helpers and sent a bowl of it to Ali. When his wife asked whether there was nothing in it for them, he said: where were you all day? Take what is left. What was left was a purse of about a thousand dirhams.

**The statement:**
> فَقَالَ لَهَا: رَحِمَكِ اللهُ، إِنَّكِ مُوَفَّقَةٌ بِنْتُ مُوَفَّقٍ، وَهِيَ أُمُّ كُلْثُوْم بِنْتُ الصِّدِّيْقِ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۱ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1457
> *English:* "He said to her: God have mercy on you, you are rightly-guided, the daughter of a rightly-guided man — and she was أم كلثوم, the daughter of الصديق."

**عبرت:** The counsel that unties a knot often comes from inside the house, not from the assembly.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF9 · An estate worth three hundred thousand, given to a stranger
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in Uthman's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** A bedouin came to Talha asking, and pressed his claim by naming a tie of kinship between them. Talha told him that nobody had ever asked him by that particular tie before. He owned a piece of land for which Uthman had offered him three hundred thousand; the man could take the land, or Talha would sell it to Uthman and hand him the price. The man asked for the price. Talha gave it to him.

**The statement:**
> فَقَالَ: إِنَّ هَذِهِ لَرَحِمٌ مَا سَأَلَنِي بِهَا أَحَدٌ قَبْلَكَ، إِنَّ لِي أَرْضاً قَدْ أَعْطَانِي بِهَا عُثْمَانُ ثَلاَثَ مَائَةِ أَلْفٍ، فَاقْبَضْهَا، وَإِنْ شِئْتَ بِعْتُهَا مِنْ عُثْمَانَ، وَدَفَعْتُ إِلَيْكَ الثَّمَنَ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۱ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1457
> *English:* "He said: this is indeed a tie of kinship by which no one has asked me before you. I have a piece of land for which عثمان offered me three hundred thousand — take it; and if you wish I will sell it to عثمان and hand you the price."

**عبرت:** A claim of kinship that has never been used is the one that should be honoured most carefully.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF10 · Four hundred thousand a year, and ten thousand to Aisha
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in Uthman's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Iraq and al-Sarat light on the map.

**What happened:** Ibn Saad set down Talha's income in plain figures: four hundred thousand a year out of Iraq, and about ten thousand dinars out of al-Sarat. And every year, when the crop came in, he sent ten thousand of it to the Mother of the Believers Aisha. The room should hear the figures and the standing gift together, because the second is what the first was for.

**The statement:**
> none in the sources we use

**عبرت:** Regular giving, fixed to the harvest and never announced, is a harder discipline than one large gift.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF11 · We temporised in the matter of Uthman
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The hardest sentence in Talha's biography is his own. After Uthman was killed, Talha said that they had temporised in his affair, and that he could find nothing better now than to spend their own blood in it, and he asked God to take from him for Uthman that day until He was satisfied. Ibn Saad carries it, and the printed edition notes an unnamed link in the chain, so it is recorded rather than asserted. The speaker states it as the book states it, attributes it to the book, and adds nothing.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ طَلْحَةُ: إِنَّا دَاهَنَّا فِي أَمْرِ عُثْمَانَ، فَلاَ نَجِدُ اليَوْمَ أَمْثَلَ مِنْ أَنْ نَبْذُلَ دِمَاءنَا فِيْهِ، اللَّهُمَّ خُذْ لِعُثْمَانَ مِنِّي اليَوْمَ حَتَّى تَرْضَى (٤) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1461
> *English:* "طلحة said: We temporised in the affair of عثمان, and today we find nothing better than to spend our own blood in it. O God, take from me for عثمان today until You are satisfied."

**عبرت:** A man who names his own failing before anyone else names it has already begun to answer for it.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF12 · Al-Dhahabi's own sentence, and the guardrail
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** This is the safe form, and it belongs to a Sunni authority rather than to us. Al-Dhahabi says in his own voice that what came from Talha in the matter of Uthman was inadvertence and agitating, that he did it by ijtihad, that he changed when he saw Uthman killed and regretted not having come to his aid, and he says may God be pleased with them both. He then adds the fact that follows from it: Talha was the first man to pledge allegiance to Ali, and the killers of Uthman pressed him hard and brought him until he pledged. Quote him; do not improve on him.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: الَّذِي كَانَ مِنْهُ فِي حَقِّ عُثْمَانَ تَمَغْفُلٌ وَتَأْليبٌ، فَعَلَهُ بِاجْتِهَادٍ، ثُمَّ تَغَيَّرَ عِنْدَمَا شَاهَدَ مَصْرَعَ عُثْمَانَ، فَنَدِمَ عَلَى تَرْكِ نُصْرَتِهِ -رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُمَا- وَكَانَ طَلْحَةُ أَوَّلَ مَنْ بَايَعَ عَلِيّاً، أَرْهَقَهُ قَتَلَةُ عُثْمَانَ، وَأَحْضَرُوهُ حَتَّى بَايَعَ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1461
> *English:* "I say: what came from him in the matter of عثمان was inadvertence and agitating — he did it by ijtihad; then he changed when he witnessed the killing of عثمان, and regretted having failed to come to his aid, may God be pleased with them both. And طلحة was the first to pledge to علي; the killers of عثمان pressed him and brought him until he pledged."

**عبرت:** When the great scholars of the ummah have already chosen their words for a hard matter, using their words is safer than choosing our own.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF13 · Turning aside at Dhat Irq to send the boys home
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** The road from Mecca towards Basra; Dhat Irq lights.

**What happened:** When Talha and al-Zubayr and Aisha went out seeking the blood of Uthman, they turned aside on the road at Dhat Irq. Two young men were with the party: Urwa, al-Zubayr's own son, and Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman. The company judged them too young for what lay ahead and sent them both back. It is a small scene and it tells the room two things at once: where the road ran, and that the men riding it knew exactly what they were riding towards.

**The statement:**
> لَمَّا خَرَجَ طَلْحَةُ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ، وَعَائِشَةُ لِلطَّلَبِ بِدَمِ عُثْمَانَ، عَرَّجُوا عَنْ مُنْصَرَفِهِمْ بِذَاتِ عِرْقٍ، فَاسْتَصْغَرُوا عُرْوَةَ بنَ الزُّبَيْرِ، وَأَبَا بَكْرٍ بنَ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ، فَرَدُّوْهُمَا.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1460
> *English:* "When طلحة and الزبير and عائشة went out to seek the blood of عثمان, they turned aside on their way at ذات عرق, and judged عروة بن الزبير and أبا بكر بن عبد الرحمن too young, and sent the two of them back."

**عبرت:** Men who send their own sons home before a march know what the march is.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF14 · Yesterday one hand, today two mountains of iron
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights.

**What happened:** On the day itself a man named Alqama found Talha and reproached him. Talha's answer is the single most quotable sentence any Companion says in this window. Yesterday, he said, we were one hand against whoever was not of us; today we have become two mountains of iron, each crawling towards the other. And then he named what he believed he owed: something had come from him in the matter of Uthman whose expiation he could see in nothing but the spilling of his own blood, and the seeking of Uthman's. The printed edition's note calls the chain good.

**The statement:**
> فَقَالَ: يَا عَلْقَمَةَ! لاَ تَلُمْنِي، كُنَّا أَمْسِ يَداً وَاحِدَةً عَلَى مَنْ سِوَانَا، فَأَصْبَحْنَا اليَوْمَ جَبَلَيْنِ مِنْ حَدِيْدٍ، يَزْحَفُ أَحَدُنَا إِلَى صَاحِبِهِ، وَلَكِنَّهُ كَانَ مِنِّي شَيْءٌ فِي أَمْرِ عُثْمَانَ مِمَّا لاَ أَرَى كَفَّارَتَهُ إِلاَّ سَفْكَ دَمِي، وَطَلَبَ دَمِهِ (٣) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1460
> *English:* "He said: علقمة, do not blame me. Yesterday we were one hand against whoever was not of us, and today we have become two mountains of iron, one of us crawling towards the other. But there was something from me in the matter of عثمان whose expiation I see in nothing but the spilling of my own blood, and the seeking of his."

**عبرت:** The men in that field were not strangers to each other, and that is exactly what made the day terrible.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF15 · A crowd that would not fall silent
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** On the day of the Camel, Talha called the people to listen to him and they would not go quiet. He gave up on them with one contemptuous line: moths of the fire, flies of greed. The men whose chains carry it are reliable. It is worth telling because it shows what the leaders on that field were actually dealing with: a crowd that had its own momentum and would not be talked down by anyone.

**The statement:**
> فَقَالَ: أُفٍّ! فَرَاشُ النَّارِ، وَذُبابُ طَمَعٍ (٣) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1461
> *English:* "He said: Ugh! Moths of the fire, and flies of greed."

**عبرت:** A crowd that will not listen has already taken the decision out of the hands of the men it is following.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF16 · Marwan's arrow, and a knee that would not stop bleeding
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights.

**What happened:** Talha was not killed by the other army. Qays reported that he saw Marwan ibn al-Hakam shoot him that day with an arrow which struck him in the knee, and it bled and bled until he died. The printed edition calls that chain sound. Yahya ibn Bukayr, Khalifa ibn Khayyat and Abu Nasr al-Kalabadhi all name the same man as the killer. The speaker reports the three names, and stops there; the arrow is not turned into an argument about anybody's dynasty.

**The statement:**
> رَأَيْتُ مَرْوَانَ بنَ الحَكَمِ حِيْنَ رَمَى طَلْحَةَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِسَهْمٍ، فَوَقَعَ فِي رُكْبَتِهِ، فَمَا زَالَ يَنْسَحُّ حَتَّى
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1461
> *English:* "I saw مروان بن الحكم when he shot طلحة that day with an arrow, and it fell in his knee, and it did not stop bleeding until …"

**عبرت:** In a fitna the deadliest arrow can come from a man's own side, which is one reason the books call such a day a fitna.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF17 · Al-Dhahabi weighs the killer of Talha
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabi does not leave the matter of the killer to the room's imagination. He states his own judgement in a single short sentence, and it is deliberately even-handed: the killer of Talha stands, in the burden of sin, in the same place as the killer of Ali. That is the sentence to have ready when someone in the hall wants the platform to say more.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: قَاتِلُ طَلْحَةَ فِي الوِزْرِ، بِمَنْزِلَةِ قَاتِلِ عَلِيٍّ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1462
> *English:* "I say: the killer of طلحة stands, in the burden of sin, in the same place as the killer of علي."

**عبرت:** The same measure applied to both sides is what makes a verdict trustworthy.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF18 · Ali gets down from his mount and wipes the dust away
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, after al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights.

**What happened:** After the fighting, Ali came upon Talha lying thrown down in a valley. He dismounted, wiped the dust from his face, and spoke to the dead man by his kunya: it is hard on me, Abu Muhammad, that I should see you laid low in the valleys beneath the stars of heaven. Then he said he complained of his griefs to God. If the room is to carry one picture out of the day of the Camel, this is the one it should carry.

**The statement:**
> رَأَى عَلِيٌّ طَلْحَةَ فِي وَادٍ مُلْقَى، فَنَزَلَ، فَمَسَحَ التُّرَابَ عَنْ وَجْهِهِ، وَقَالَ: عَزِيْزٌ عَلَيَّ أَبَا مُحَمَّدٍ بِأَنْ أَرَاكَ مُجَدَّلاً فِي الأَوْدِيَةِ تَحْتَ نُجُومِ السَّمَاءِ، إِلَى اللهِ أَشْكُو عُجَرِي وَبُجَرِي.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۳۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1462
> *English:* "علي saw طلحة lying thrown down in a valley, so he dismounted and wiped the dust from his face and said: it is hard on me, أبا محمد, that I should see you laid low in the valleys beneath the stars of heaven. To God I complain of my sorrows, the hidden and the plain."

**عبرت:** Men who fought each other that morning were still brothers to each other that evening, and the books never pretended otherwise.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF19 · A son killed on the same field as his father
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Talha's son Muhammad, born in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ was killed at the Camel on the same day as his father. Ali grieved for him, and said of him a line that is both an epitaph and an explanation: his devotion to his father laid him low. The young man had no quarrel of his own on that field; he was there because his father was.

**The statement:**
> وُلِدَ فِي حَيَاةِ النَّبِيِّ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- قُتِلَ يَوْمَ الجَمَلِ أَيْضاً، فَحَزِنَ عَلَيْهِ عَلِيٌّ وَقَالَ: صَرَعَهُ بِرُّهُ بِأَبِيْهِ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۰ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1466
> *English:* "He was born in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and was killed on the day of الجمل also; علي grieved for him and said: his devotion to his father laid him low."

**عبرت:** A quarrel among elders is paid for by young men who were never part of it.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF20 · Three hundred camel-loads of gold, and a scholar's refusal
**Tier:** CUT · **When:** recorded, not planned `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** A figure circulates that Talha left behind three hundred camel-loads of gold. Al-Dhahabi meets it head-on: he says the most astonishing thing that has ever come before him is Ibn al-Jawzi's saying that. The card exists so that the figure is never repeated from this platform and never researched again. If somebody in the hall produces it, the answer is that the author of the Siyar refused it, and the estate figures the book does give are on the same page.

**The statement:**
> أَعْجَبُ مَا مَرَّ بِي قَوْلُ ابْنِ الجَوْزِيِّ فِي كَلاَمٍ لَهُ عَلَى حَدِيْثٍ قَالَ: وَقَدْ خَلَّفَ طَلْحَةُ ثَلاَثَ مَائَةِ حِمْلٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۰ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1466
> *English:* "The most astonishing thing that has passed before me is the saying of ابن الجوزي, in something he said about a حديث: طلحة left behind three hundred camel-loads of gold."

**عبرت:** A number nobody checked travels further than one that was checked, which is why the scholars checked them.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF21 · The year of his death, and what the books disagree about
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** Jumada al-Akhira 36 AH, or Rajab `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights; the grave outside the town.

**What happened:** The Siyar gives the death in Jumada al-Akhira of the year 36, and says it is also said Rajab, at an age of about sixty-two, and that he was buried outside Basra. Al-Tabarani has a report that he was sixty-four and buried inside Basra in the quarter of Thaqif, but the printed edition notes al-Waqidi in its chain and that he is abandoned. This is what a real disagreement looks like in a serious book: both readings are written down, and the weaker chain is named as weaker rather than quietly dropped.

**The statement:**
> none in the sources we use

**عبرت:** A book that records its own uncertainty is more trustworthy than one that records only a single tidy answer.

**Hands-up?** no

**الزبير بن العوام ؓ — E-PF22 to E-PF47**

### POT/E-PF22 · The Prophet's cousin, and the first sword drawn
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** before 23 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabi heads this life with the titles the tradition itself gave, and every one of them is a fact rather than a compliment. Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam was the hawari of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the son of his paternal aunt Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib; one of the ten given the good news of Paradise; one of the six of the shura; and the first man to draw his sword in the way of God. He accepted Islam as a youth of sixteen. His wife was Asma bint Abi Bakr, which makes Aisha his sister-in-law and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr her nephew.

**The statement:**
> حَوَارِيُّ رَسُوْلِ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- وَابْنُ عَمَّتِهِ صَفِيَّةَ بِنْتِ عَبْدِ المُطَّلِبِ، وَأَحَدُ العَشرَةِ المَشْهُوْدِ لَهُم بِالجَنَّةِ، وَأَحَدُ (١) السِّتَّةِ أَهْلِ الشُّوْرَى، وَأَوَّلُ مَنْ سَلَّ سَيْفَهُ فِي سَبِيْلِ اللهِ، أَبُو عَبْدِ اللهِ -رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنْهُ- أَسْلَمَ وَهُوَ حَدَثٌ، لَهُ سِتَّ (٢) عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۱ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1467
> *English:* "The حواري of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the son of his paternal aunt صفية بنت عبد المطلب; one of the ten given the good news of الجنة; one of the six of the شورى; and the first to draw his sword in the way of God — أبو عبد الله رضي الله عنه. He accepted Islam while a youth, sixteen years old."

**عبرت:** A man's standing in this story is established by the titles the ummah already gave him, not by any we might reach for.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF23 · Every prophet has a hawari, and mine is al-Zubayr
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 5 AH, the Trench `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina; the trench line on its northern side.

**What happened:** On the day of the Trench the Prophet ﷺ asked who would go and bring back news of Banu Qurayza. Al-Zubayr said: I will. He asked again, and al-Zubayr said: I will. He asked a third time, and al-Zubayr said: I will. It was then that the Prophet ﷺ said the sentence the ummah has remembered ever since. Al-Bukhari and Muslim both carry it.

**The statement:**
> فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-: (لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ حَوَارِيٌّ، وَحَوَارِيَّ الزُّبَيْرُ (١)) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۸ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1474
> *English:* "The Prophet ﷺ said: every prophet has a حواري, and my حواري is الزبير."

**عبرت:** A man who answers the third time as readily as the first is the one worth sending.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF24 · The son of my aunt, and my hawari from my ummah
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** before 23 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The Siyar carries a second wording of the same praise, and this one names the kinship as well as the office. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that al-Zubayr was the son of his paternal aunt, and his hawari from his ummah. The two facts belong together: this was family, and this was also the man sent when a thing had to be found out.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ رَسُوْلُ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-: (الزُّبَيْرُ ابْنُ عَمَّتِي، وَحَوَارِيَّ مِنْ أُمَّتِي (٣)) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۸ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1474
> *English:* "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: الزبير is the son of my paternal aunt, and my حواري from my ummah."

**عبرت:** Closeness of blood did not excuse a man from the errand; it was usually what got him sent.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF25 · A boy runs through Mecca with a drawn sword
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** before the hijra `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Mecca lights.

**What happened:** Al-Zubayr accepted Islam extremely young. Al-Dhahabi's own heading says sixteen; his son Urwa's report says he was eight when he became Muslim, and that at twelve a rumour ran through Mecca that the Prophet ﷺ had been seized, and the boy came out through the lanes with his sword already drawn. The Prophet ﷺ met him and asked him what was the matter. That is the first picture the room gets of him, and it explains every later one.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ عُرْوَةُ: جَاءَ الزُّبَيْرُ بِسَيْفِهِ، فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-: (مَا لَكَ؟) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1471
> *English:* "عروة said: الزبير came with his sword, and the Prophet ﷺ said: what is the matter with you?"

**عبرت:** A disposition shows itself early and does not change; the books simply record where it first showed.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF26 · Five of these men entered Islam at one man's hand
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** before the hijra `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Mecca lights.

**What happened:** Ibn Ishaq reports that five of the men this session is about entered Islam at the hand of Abu Bakr: al-Zubayr, Uthman, Talha, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Saad. Four of them would sit in the shura of the year 23, and three of them would be dead by the year 36. One sentence organises the whole board for the room: these were not strangers who happened to collide, they were men brought into the religion by the same person.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ ابْنُ إِسْحَاقَ: وَأَسْلَمَ - عَلَى مَا بَلَغَنِي - عَلَى يَدِ أَبِي بَكْرٍ: الزُّبَيْرُ، وَعُثْمَانُ، وَطَلْحَةُ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ، وَسَعْدٌ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1471
> *English:* "ابن إسحاق said: and there accepted Islam — according to what has reached me — at the hand of أبي بكر: الزبير, and عثمان, and طلحة, and عبد الرحمن, and سعد."

**عبرت:** Men who begin together can still end on opposite sides of a field, and that is what makes a fitna a fitna.

**Hands-up?** Of the men we will meet tonight, how many came into Islam through أبو بكر ؓ?

### POT/E-PF27 · Two horsemen at Badr, and he was one of them
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 2 AH, Badr `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Badr lights.

**What happened:** The whole Muslim army at Badr had two men on horseback. Al-Zubayr was on the right wing and al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad on the left. The detail is worth a sentence because it sets the scale of the beginning against the scale of everything the session is about to cover: within a single lifetime the same community would be arguing over the government of Egypt, Iraq and Persia.

**The statement:**
> كَانَ يَوْمَ بَدْرٍ مَعَ رَسُوْلِ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- فَارِسَانِ: الزُّبَيْرُ عَلَى فَرَسٍ، عَلَى المَيْمَنَةِ، وَالمِقْدَادُ بنُ الأَسْوَدِ عَلَى فَرَسٍ، عَلَى المَيْسَرَةِ (٢) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1472
> *English:* "On the day of بدر there were two horsemen with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: الزبير on a horse, on the right wing, and المقداد بن الأسود on a horse, on the left wing."

**عبرت:** Everything the room will hear tonight grew out of a community that once fielded two horses.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF28 · Who will bring us news of Banu Qurayza
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 5 AH, the Trench `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina; Banu Qurayza's quarter to the south-east.

**What happened:** The question itself is worth a card, because it is the moment the hawari saying was earned. On the day of the Trench, with the city surrounded, the Prophet ﷺ asked: who will bring us news of Banu Qurayza? Going meant riding out alone, past the besieging army, to a quarter that had just broken its agreement. Al-Zubayr volunteered three times.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ رَسُوْلُ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- يَوْمَ الخَنْدَقِ: (مَنْ يَأْتِيْنَا بِخَبَرِ بَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ؟) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۴۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1473
> *English:* "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day of الخندق: who will bring us news of بني قريظة?"

**عبرت:** The errand nobody volunteers for is the one that decides the day.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF29 · Three sword-cuts, and a shoulder a child could put fingers into
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** by 15 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Badr and Yarmuk light in turn.

**What happened:** His son Urwa said there were three sword-cuts in his father's body. One of them was in the shoulder, and Urwa said that as a child he used to put his fingers into it. Two of the three were taken at Badr and one at Yarmuk. The room hears in one sentence that this was a man of the first battle and of the conquest of Syria both.

**The statement:**
> مَعْمَرٌ: عَنْ هِشَامٍ، عَنْ (٣) عُرْوَةَ قَالَ: كَانَ فِي الزُّبَيْرِ ثَلاَثُ ضَرَبَاتٍ بِالسَّيْفِ: إِحْدَاهُنَّ فِي عَاتِقِهِ، إِنْ كُنْتُ لأُدْخِلُ أَصَابِعِي فِيْهَا، ضُرِب ثِنْتَيْنِ يَوْمَ بَدْرٍ، وَوَاحِدَةً يَوْمَ اليَرْمُوْكِ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۵۲ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1478
> *English:* "عروة said: there were three sword-cuts in الزبير; one of them was in his shoulder — I used to put my fingers into it. Two were struck on the day of بدر, and one on the day of اليرموك."

**عبرت:** The body of one Companion can carry the whole first forty years of this history on it.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF30 · He struck his own name off the register
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 23 AH, and again 35 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina lights.

**What happened:** When Umar was killed, al-Zubayr erased his own name from the diwan, the state register of stipends. When Uthman was killed, his son Abdullah did exactly the same thing. Two generations, the same gesture, twelve years apart: a refusal to be carried on the books of a government whose head had just been murdered.

**The statement:**
> اللَّيْثُ: عَنْ هِشَامِ بنِ عُرْوَةَ: أَنَّ الزُّبَيْرَ لَمَّا قُتِلَ عُمَرُ، مَحَا نَفْسَهُ مِنَ الدِّيْوَانِ، وَأَنَّ ابْنَهُ عَبْدَ اللهِ لَمَّا قُتِلَ عُثْمَانُ، مَحَا نَفْسَهُ مِنَ الدِّيْوَانِ (٢) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۵۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1483
> *English:* "الليث, from هشام بن عروة: that الزبير, when عمر was killed, struck his own name from the register; and that his son عبد الله, when عثمان was killed, struck his own name from the register."

**عبرت:** There is a way of registering dissent that costs the man himself and costs nobody else anything.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF31 · Uthman's oath about the man they were naming after him
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in Uthman's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** In the year Uthman was ill and bleeding at the nose, he was pressed to name a successor and told that the people were saying al-Zubayr. His answer was an oath: by Him in whose hand is my soul, he was the best of them as far as I knew, and the most beloved of them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Bukhari carries it and the printed edition calls the chain sound. Keep this card close to the cards about the day of the Camel, because it is the same two men.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ: أَمَا وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ، إِنْ كَانَ لأَخْيَرَهُمْ (٢) مَا عَلِمْتُ، وَأَحَبَّهُم إِلَى رَسُوْلِ اللهِ (٣) -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۵۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1480
> *English:* "He said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, he was the best of them as far as I knew, and the most beloved of them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

**عبرت:** What a man says of another when there is nothing to be gained by saying it is the testimony worth keeping.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF32 · Seven Companions made him executor of their estates
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** by 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Seven of the Companions made al-Zubayr the executor of their wills, among them Uthman, Ibn Masud and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. He would spend on their heirs out of his own property and keep theirs intact. This is the single most useful fact about him for a room that is about to hear about the day of the Camel: he was the man the others trusted with their children's money.

**The statement:**
> أَوْصَى إِلَى الزُّبَيْرِ سَبْعَةٌ مِنَ الصَّحَابَةِ، مِنْهُم: عُثْمَانُ، وَابْنُ مَسْعُوْدٍ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ، فَكَانَ يُنْفِقُ عَلَى الوَرَثَةِ مِنْ مَالِهِ، وَيَحْفَظُ أَمْوَالَهُمْ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۵۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1481
> *English:* "Seven of the Companions made الزبير the executor of their estates — among them عثمان, and ابن مسعود, and عبد الرحمن — and he would spend on the heirs out of his own property, and guard their property."

**عبرت:** The office nobody campaigns for is given to the man everyone has already decided to trust.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF33 · A thousand slaves paying tribute, and none of it came home
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in this window `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Awzai's chain reports that al-Zubayr had a thousand slaves who paid him a tribute out of their earnings, and that he would not bring a single thing of that tribute into his own house. > *English:* "الزبير بن العوام had a thousand slaves who paid him tribute, and he would not bring a thing of their tribute into his house."

**عبرت:** Income a man refuses to let through his own door is the plainest test of what he thinks it is for.

### POT/E-PF34 · I came out only for the thrust and the plague
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in this window `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Egypt lights.

> *English:* "He said: I came out only for the thrust and the plague. So he entered it, and met a thrust in his forehead, and recovered."

**عبرت:** A man who has already settled with himself how he expects to die is not easily governed by warnings.

### POT/E-PF35 · We used to recite the verse and think it was about others
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** A man put the hardest question of the year to al-Zubayr's face: what brought you here? You let the Caliph be killed and then came seeking his blood. Al-Zubayr did not argue. He said they had been reciting the verse warning of a fitna that does not strike only the wrongdoers among them, all through the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and of Abu Bakr and Umar and Uthman, and they never supposed they were its people, until it fell among them where it fell. The printed edition calls the chain good.

**The statement:**
> قَالَ: إِنَّا قَرَأْنَا عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُوْلِ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- وَأَبِي بَكْرٍ، وَعُمَرَ، وَعُثْمَانَ: {وَاتَّقُوا فِتْنَةً لاَ تُصِيْبَنَّ الَّذِيْنَ ظَلَمُوا مِنْكُمْ خَاصَّةً} [الأَنْفَال: ٢٥] لَمْ نَكُنْ نَحْسِبُ أَنَّا أَهْلُهَا حَتَّى وَقَعَتْ مِنَّا حَيْثُ وَقَعَتْ (٣) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۵۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1483
> *English:* "He said: We used to recite in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and of أبي بكر, and عمر, and عثمان — {And beware of a fitna that will not strike only those of you who did wrong} [الأنفال 25] — and we did not think that we were its people, until it fell among us where it fell."

**عبرت:** The warnings a community recites for years are usually understood to be about somebody else.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF36 · No one is killed today but a wrongdoer or one wronged
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH, the morning of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights.

**What happened:** On the morning of the battle al-Zubayr spoke to his son Abdullah. He said that nobody would be killed that day except a wrongdoer or one wronged, and that he did not see himself as anything but a man who would be killed that day wronged. Then, in the same breath, he turned to the thing that was actually weighing on him: his debt, and whether it would leave anything at all of the family property. Al-Bukhari carries the long version and the printed edition calls its men reliable.

**The statement:**
> يَا بُنَيَّ! إِنَّهُ لاَ يُقْتَلُ اليَوْمَ إِلاَّ ظَالِمٌ أَوْ مَظْلُوْمٌ، وَإِنِّي لاَ أُرَانِي إِلاَّ سَأُقْتَلُ اليَوْمَ مَظْلُوْماً، وَإِنَّ مِنْ أَكْبَرِ هَمِّي لَدَيْنِي، أَفَتَرَى دَيْنَنَا يُبْقِي مِنْ مَالِنَا شَيْئاً؟
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1491
> *English:* "My son — no one is killed today but a wrongdoer or one wronged, and I do not see myself as anything but one who will be killed today wronged. And the heaviest of my cares is my debt. Do you think our debt will leave anything of our property?"

**عبرت:** A man on the morning of a battle worries about the debts he owes, not about the argument he is in.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF37 · Al-Zubayr turns away from the field
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Basra lights; one rider leaves the field.

**What happened:** This is to be told exactly as the books tell it and no further. At the Camel, Ali called al-Zubayr out between the two lines and reminded him of something he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Zubayr then withdrew from the battle and rode away. The wording of the reminder is carried in more than one form and the printed edition grades those forms differently, so the speaker says only what all of them agree on: he was reminded, and he withdrew.

> none in the sources we use

### POT/E-PF38 · Cowardice, said his son; and the answer he gave
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

### POT/E-PF39 · The line of verse he recited as he rode away
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH, the day of al-Jamal `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** The road out of Basra towards Wadi al-Siba.

**What happened:** Having answered his son, al-Zubayr recited a single line of verse and rode off: to leave the matters whose consequences he feared, for the sake of God, was better in this world and in religion. He had barely gone before Ibn Jarmuz killed him. The line and the killing belong on the same card, because the room must feel that withdrawing did not save him.

> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۰ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1486
> *English:* "To leave the matters whose consequences I fear, for God's sake, is better in this world and in religion."

**عبرت:** Withdrawing from a wrong does not guarantee safety; it only settles what a man will answer for.

### POT/E-PF40 · Killed at Wadi al-Siba, and Ali sat and wept
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Wadi al-Siba, seven farsakhs from Basra.

**What happened:** Umayr ibn Jarmuz, Fadala ibn Habis and a man called Nufay went after him. Umayr came at him from behind and gave him a weak thrust; al-Zubayr turned on him, and Umayr called the other two in. The second thrust finished him. He was buried at Wadi al-Siba, seven farsakhs from Basra. And Ali sat down and wept over him, he and his companions.

**عبرت:** The men of that generation grieved for the men they had just been opposite, and the books recorded the grief as carefully as the fighting.

### POT/E-PF41 · Give the killer of the son of Safiyya the tidings of the Fire
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** When the head of al-Zubayr was brought to Ali, he did not receive it as a victory. He told the man to take his seat in the Fire, and said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had told him that the killer of al-Zubayr is in the Fire. ### POT/E-PF42 · Not for the thong of his sandal

### POT/E-PF43 · Al-Dhahabi distinguishes one killer from the others
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** a scholar's verdict `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Dhahabi allows himself a comment on the killer of al-Zubayr, and it is careful. He says the wretch ate his own hands in remorse for killing him and asked forgiveness — unlike the killer of Talha, the killer of Uthman and the killer of Ali. He is not excusing the man; he is distinguishing between four crimes that a careless speaker would run together.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: أَكَلَ المُعَثَّرُ يَدَيْهِ نَدَماً عَلَى قَتْلِهِ، وَاسْتَغْفَرَ لاَ كَقَاتِلِ طَلْحَةَ، وَقَاتِلِ عُثْمَانَ، وَقَاتِلِ عَلِيٍّ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1490
> *English:* "I say: the wretch ate his own hands in remorse for killing him, and he asked forgiveness — not like the killer of طلحة, and the killer of عثمان, and the killer of علي."

**عبرت:** Even in judging the worst act of a year, the scholars refused to judge four men with one sentence.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF44 · The refusal that lets the platform decline to judge
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** a scholar's verdict `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** A report is transmitted from al-Hasan that Ali, after the Camel, spoke of a leader of fitna who entered Paradise while his followers went to the Fire, and named al-Zubayr. Al-Dhahabi does not pass it on and move away. He rejects both its chain and its wording, and then states the Sunni position on all three armies in one sentence: God forbid that we should testify against the followers of al-Zubayr, or the army of Muawiya, or of Ali, that they are in the Fire; rather we consign their affair to God and ask forgiveness for them. Read it out as his, by name.

**The statement:**
> فِي إِسْنَادِهِ إِرْسَالٌ، وَفِي لَفْظِهِ نَكَارَةٌ، فَمَعَاذَ الله أَنْ نَشْهَدَ عَلَى أَتْبَاعِ الزُّبَيْرِ، أَوْ جُنْدِ مُعَاوِيَةَ، أَوْ عَلِيٍّ، بِأَنَّهُمْ فِي النَّارِ، بَلْ نُفَوِّضُ أَمْرَهُمْ إِلَى اللهِ، وَنَسْتَغْفِرُ لَهُمْ، بَلَى: الخَوَارِجُ كِلاَبُ النَّارِ، وَشَرُّ قَتْلَى تَحْتَ أَدِيْمِ السَّمَاءِ، لأَنَّهُمْ مَرَقُوا مِنَ الإِسْلاَمِ، ثُمَّ لاَ نَدْرِيْ مَصِيْرَهُمْ إِلَى مَاذَا، وَلاَ نَحْكُمُ عَلَيْهِم بِخُلُوْدِ النَّارِ، بَلْ نَقِفُ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۳ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1489
> *English:* "In its chain there is إرسال, and in its wording there is نكارة. God forbid that we should testify against the followers of الزبير, or the army of معاوية, or of علي, that they are in the Fire. Rather we consign their affair to God, and ask forgiveness for them. Yes — the خوارج are the dogs of the Fire and the worst slain under the vault of heaven, because they passed clean out of Islam; then we do not know what their end is, and we do not rule that they abide in the Fire for ever, but we stop."

**عبرت:** The scholars of this ummah settled long ago that the right response to that year is to consign it to God and ask forgiveness, and that settlement is not ours to reopen.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF45 · Why we love them, and whom we do not
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** a scholar's verdict `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** A page before the refusal, al-Dhahabi has already given the reason behind it. These men are of the ten given the good news of Paradise, of the men of Badr, of the people of the Pledge of Ridwan, and of the first forerunners of whom God announced that He was pleased with them and they with Him; and the four of them were killed and granted martyrdom. So, he says, we love them, and we hate the four who killed the four. That is the whole frame of the evening in two clauses.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: لأَنَّهُم مِنَ العَشْرَةِ المَشْهُوْدِ لَهُم بِالجَنَّةِ، وَمِنَ البَدْرِيِّيْنَ، وَمِنْ أَهْلِ بَيْعَةِ الرِّضْوَانِ، وَمِنَ السَّابِقِيْنَ الأَوَّلِيْنَ الَّذِيْنَ أَخْبَرَ تَعَالَى أَنَّهُ رَضِيَ عَنْهُم وَرَضُوْا عَنْهُ، وَلأَنَّ الأَرْبَعَةَ قُتِلُوا وَرُزِقُوا الشَّهَادَةَ، فَنَحْنُ مُحِبُّوْنَ لَهُم، بَاغِضُوْنَ لِلأَرْبَعَةِ الَّذِيْنَ قَتَلُوا الأَرْبَعَةَ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۲ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1488
> *English:* "I say: because they are of the ten given the good news of الجنة, and of the men of بدر, and of the people of بيعة الرضوان, and of the first forerunners of whom God Most High announced that He was pleased with them and they with Him; and because the four of them were killed and granted martyrdom. So we love them, and we hate the four who killed the four."

**عبرت:** The verdict of the Qur'an on these men was given before the quarrel, and it is not undone by the quarrel.

### POT/E-PF46 · No dinar and no dirham, and a debt of two million two hundred thousand
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH and after `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina, Basra, Kufa, Egypt light together.

**What happened:** When Abdullah settled his father's estate he found that al-Zubayr had left behind no dinar and no dirham — only land at al-Ghaba and houses in Medina, Basra, Kufa and Egypt. The reason was a scruple: when a man brought him money to keep, al-Zubayr refused to take it as a deposit and took it as a loan instead, so that if it were lost he would owe it. Abdullah reckoned the debt and found it two million two hundred thousand. He then stood at the pilgrimage season four years running calling on any creditor to come forward, before he would divide the inheritance at all.

**The statement:**
> فَحَسَبْتُ دَيْنَهُ، فَوَجَدْتُهُ أَلْفَي أَلْفٍ وَمَائَتَي أَلْفٍ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۶ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1492
> *English:* "So I reckoned his debt, and I found it two million two hundred thousand."

**عبرت:** A man who refuses to hold money on terms that could leave the owner unpaid will die owing a fortune and leaving no one cheated.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF47 · How old was he, and why the books do not agree
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Al-Waqidi and Ibn Numayr say al-Zubayr was sixty-four when he was killed. Others say he was fifty-odd. Al-Dhahabi records both and then adds two words of his own: and that is the more likely. This is a small card that does a large job, because it shows the room what a careful historian does when his sources differ — he prints both, says which he prefers, and does not pretend the difference away.

**The statement:**
> وَقَالَ غَيْرُهُمَا: قِيْلَ: وَلَهُ بِضْعٌ وَخَمْسُوْنَ سَنَةً، وَهُوَ أَشْبَهُ.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۱ ص۶۴ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/1490
> *English:* "And others than those two said: it is said, he was fifty-odd years old — and that is the more likely."

**عبرت:** An author who tells you which of two reports he prefers, and why, has given you more than one who gives you a single confident number.

**Hands-up?** no

The room should meet her as a jurist before it meets her on a road to Basra, because that is the order the book itself uses.

> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۳۵ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2115
> *English:* "The Mother of the Believers, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, the most learned in fiqh of all the women of the ummah, without qualification."

**عبرت:** A person's standing is fixed by what they knew and taught, and it is not cancelled by one journey they later regretted.

### POT/E-PF49 · The kinship map that explains who stood where
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina; then the road to Basra.

**What happened:** Before the day of the Camel is described at all, the room needs four family facts and no interpretation on top of them. Aisha was of Banu Taym, the daughter of Abu Bakr. Talha was of Banu Taym too, and his wife Umm Kulthum was her own sister. Her other sister Asma was the wife of al-Zubayr, so al-Zubayr was her brother-in-law and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr her nephew. That is the whole explanation of who rode with whom, and it needs nothing added.

**The statement:**
> none in the sources we use

**عبرت:** Most of what looks like faction in this year is family, and saying so plainly removes more heat than any argument would.

### POT/E-PF50 · Do not hurt me in the matter of Aisha
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** before 11 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The other wives of the Prophet ﷺ sent Umm Salama to ask him to spread the gifts people brought evenly, rather than waiting for the day he was with Aisha. She raised it with him three times. The third time he answered her, and the answer settles Aisha's place among them: do not hurt me in the matter of Aisha, for by God revelation never came down on me while I was in the blanket of any woman among you but her. Al-Bukhari and Muslim both carry it.

**The statement:**
> فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ الثَّالِثَةُ، قَالَ: (يَا أُمَّ سَلَمَةَ! لاَ تُؤْذِيْنِي فِي عَائِشَةَ، فَإِنَّهُ -وَاللهِ- مَا نَزَلَ عَلَيَّ الوَحْيُ وَأَنَا فِي لِحَافِ امْرَأَةٍ مِنْكُنَّ غَيْرِهَا) .
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۴۲ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2122
> *English:* "When it was the third time, he said: أم سلمة, do not hurt me in the matter of عائشة, for by God, revelation has never come down on me while I was in the blanket of any woman among you but her."

**عبرت:** A distinction that came from God is not a grievance to be settled among people.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF51 · Who is most beloved to you of people
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** before 11 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Amr ibn al-As asked the Prophet ﷺ who was most beloved to him of people. He said: Aisha. Amr asked: and of the men? He said: her father. Al-Dhahabi carries it and says of it in his own words that this is a sound hadith; it is in al-Bukhari and Muslim. Two lines of dialogue tell the room why this household is at the centre of everything the session is about to narrate.

**The statement:**
> أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِرَسُوْلِ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-: مَنْ أَحَبُّ النَّاسِ إِلَيْكَ؟
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۴۸ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2128
> *English:* "He said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: who is the most beloved of people to you?"

**عبرت:** The two names at the centre of this history were named together, and by the Prophet ﷺ himself.

### POT/E-PF52 · Jibril sends her his salam, and she answers it
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** before 11 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** The Prophet ﷺ said to her: Aish, this is Jibril, and he sends you his salam. She answered: and on him be peace and the mercy of God — you see what we do not see, Messenger of Allah. It is a short exchange, it is in al-Bukhari and Muslim, and it belongs in the evening because it is part of what the ummah has always understood about her.

> *English:* "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: عائش, this is جبريل, and he sends you his salām."

**عبرت:** Honour of this kind is reported plainly in the books, without ornament, and that is how it should be repeated.

### POT/E-PF53 · Her innocence came down from heaven
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 5 or 6 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina lights.

And when the verses came down clearing her, her words were that the praise belonged to God, not to any person, and not to the one standing in front of her. Al-Bukhari carries the account. > none in the sources we use

### POT/E-PF54 · Umar adds two thousand to her stipend, and says why
**Tier:** GOOD · **When:** in Umar's caliphate `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Medina lights.

**What happened:** Umar fixed ten thousand a year for each of the mothers of the believers, and then added two thousand for Aisha on top of it. When he was asked about the difference he gave a reason, not an administrative rule: she is the beloved of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The card is useful because it shows a caliph deliberately making an exception and stating openly why.

**The statement:**
> إِنَّهَا حَبِيْبَةُ رَسُوْلِ اللهِ (١) -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ-.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۹۷ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2177
> *English:* "She is the beloved of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

**عبرت:** A ruler who departs from his own rule and says plainly why is easier to trust than one who hides the exception.

**Hands-up?** no

### POT/E-PF55 · Two clauses, and not one word more
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Mecca, then the road to Basra.

**What happened:** After Uthman was killed, Aisha took a public position, and the book states it in exactly two clauses: Uthman was killed wronged; I call you to seek his blood, and to return the matter to a shura. That is the whole of her stated programme as the Siyar gives it. The speaker says those two clauses, in that order, and adds nothing to them from any other source.

**The statement:**
> أَنَّ عَائِشَةَ جَعَلَتْ تَقُوْلُ: إِنَّ عُثْمَانَ قُتِلَ مَظْلُوْماً، وَأَنَا أَدْعُوْكُمْ إِلَى الطَّلَبِ بِدَمِهِ، وَإِعَادَةِ الأَمْرِ شُوْرَى.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۷۸ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2158
> *English:* "عائشة began to say: عثمان was killed wronged, and I call you to seek his blood, and to return the matter to a شورى."

**عبرت:** When a position can be stated in two clauses, stating it in twenty is already an argument rather than a report.

### POT/E-PF56 · How will it be when the dogs of al-Hawab bark at her
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, on the road `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Al-Hawab, on the road towards Basra, lights.

**What happened:** The Siyar carries a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ said one day to his wives: how will it be with one of you when the dogs of al-Hawab bark at her? Al-Dhahabi carries the account from Ahmad's Musnad and says of it, in his own words, that this is a hadith with a sound chain which they did not include in their collections. It is narrated here as a warning that was given and remembered, and for no other purpose.

> قَالَتْ: إِنَّ رَسُوْلَ اللهِ -صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ- قَالَ ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ: (كَيْفَ بِإِحْدَاكُنَّ تَنْبُحُ عَلَيْهَا كِلاَبُ الحَوْأَبِ) ٠٢) .

### POT/E-PF57 · The night the dogs barked, and she said she would turn back
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** 36 AH, on the road `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** Al-Hawab lights on the road.

### POT/E-PF62 · Al-Dhahabi explains what she meant, and refuses to let it be read as blame
**Tier:** CORE · **When:** a scholar's verdict `[SOURCED]` · **Map:** No map.

**What happened:** Having quoted her, al-Dhahabi tells the reader in his own voice what she meant by that word, and he gives both halves of the Sunni position in one sentence. She meant her going out on the day of the Camel; she regretted it with a complete regret and repented of it; and she did not do it except as one interpreting, aiming at the good, just as Talha and al-Zubayr and a company of the great ones exercised ijtihad. May God be pleased with them all. Neither half of that sentence may be dropped.

**The statement:**
> قُلْتُ: تَعْنِي بِالحَدَثِ (٣) : مَسِيْرَهَا يَوْمَ الجَمَلِ، فَإِنَّهَا نَدِمَتْ نَدَامَةً كُلِّيَّةً، وَتَابَتْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ، عَلَى أَنَّهَا مَا فَعَلَتْ ذَلِكَ إِلاَّ مُتَأَوِّلَةً، قَاصِدَةً لِلْخَيْرِ، كَمَا اجْتَهَدَ طَلْحَةُ بنُ عُبَيْدِ اللهِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ بنُ العَوَّامِ، وَجَمَاعَةٌ مِنَ الكِبَارِ - رَضِيَ اللهُ عَنِ الجَمِيْعِ -.
> — سير أعلام النبلاء ج۲ ص۱۹۳ · https://shamela.ws/book/10906/2173
> *English:* "I say: she means by الحدث her going out on the day of الجمل, for she regretted it with a complete regret and repented of it — though she did not do it except as one interpreting, aiming at the good, just as طلحة بن عبيد الله and الزبير بن العوام and a company of the great ones exercised ijtihad. May God be pleased with them all."

**عبرت:** Repentance and good intention are not rival explanations; the tradition holds both at once and so should the platform.

**Hands-up?** no
